title: Branzino al sale
subtitle: Sea bass baked in a salt crust
excerpt: A whole sea bass packed in a thick crust of coarse salt and baked until the crust is hard and the fish inside is perfectly steamed. Broken open at the table, it reveals impeccably moist and delicately seasoned flesh.
sourceNotes: Salt-crusted fish is a preparation found throughout the Mediterranean; branzino al sale is the Italian version, most associated with coastal Liguria and Sicily. Cross-referenced with Giorgio Locatelli, Made in Italy (2006) and Anna Del Conte, Gastronomy of Italy (1987).

content.text: Branzino al sale is the Italian method for whole fish: buried in coarse sea salt, the fish steams inside an insulating crust that traps moisture. It does not make the fish salty; the salt crust creates a sealed oven-within-an-oven that produces very even, gentle cooking. The technique works best with a whole fish of about 600 to 800 g. Buy the freshest sea bass you can find; the method exposes the fish's quality with nothing to hide behind.

items.prepNote: 600 to 800 g, gutted and scaled, fins trimmed; ask the fishmonger
coarse rock salt or sea salt flakes; about 3 boxes
a few slices inside the fish, and wedges to serve

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C fan (180°C conventional, gas 6).
Mix the coarse salt with the egg whites until it looks like wet sand and holds together when pressed.
Stuff the cavity of the fish with the thyme sprigs and 2 or 3 lemon slices.
Spread a 1 cm layer of the salt mixture on a baking tray. Lay the fish on top. Pack the remaining salt firmly over and around the fish, encasing it completely. No part of the fish should be visible.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes for a 700 g fish. The salt crust will be hard and pale golden.

Bring to the table and crack the crust open with a heavy spoon or small hammer. Peel back the salt crust, pull away the skin, and lift the fillets from the bone with a spoon and fork. Serve with very good olive oil and lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The fish is overcooked and dry
items.cause: Cooked too long for its weight
items.fix: Allow 20 minutes for 600 g, 30 minutes for 800 g. When in doubt, undercook: you can return the fish to the oven for 5 more minutes if needed.

items.cause: Fine salt used instead of coarse, or cracks in the crust
items.fix: Always use coarse salt. Check the crust has no gaps before baking.

items.cause: Insufficient egg white or not enough moisture in the salt
items.fix: Add another egg white. The mixture should hold a firm shape when squeezed in your hand.

items.symptom: The fish sticks to the salt on the bottom
items.cause: The fish was baked without a base layer of salt
items.fix: Always put a layer of salt under the fish. The fillets should lift cleanly from the bone.

content.text: Salt-crusted fish is a technique with ancient roots: it appears in Roman cooking manuscripts and is found in various forms across the Mediterranean, from Spain (dorada a la sal) to Italy (branzino al sale) to Greece and Turkey. In Italy it is considered the purest way to cook a whole fish: no added fat, no aromatics beyond what is stuffed inside, nothing to interfere with the flavour of a very fresh fish. The theatrical table-side cracking of the crust is part of its appeal for dinner parties.
